subject: Activation playbook: staging cutover constraints
messages:
From: Lydia Park <lydia.park@pioneerfinancial.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
Cc: Procurement Team <procurement@pioneerfinancial.com>
Date: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:14:00 -0800
Subject: Activation playbook: staging cutover constraints

Hi Sean,

Thanks for the materials so far. As we review Redwood's proposed activation/playbook for the staging -> primary cutover we need a few clarifications to include in our RFP response pack and to raise with Procurement:

1) RTO / RPO expectations for a regional switchover (active -> failover) at the tenant level. Please provide typical and worst-case numbers and any caveats.
2) Is cross-region replication synchronous or asynchronous by default? If async, what's the typical lag and options to reduce it?
3) Cache and KV warming strategy: will we lose ephemeral session/state during failover? Any recommended warm-up steps?
4) KMS / key rollover during failover — how are encrypted token keys handled across regions?
5) What fallbacks are available if the target region cannot satisfy capacity (automated model-variant fallback, route to dedicated, etc.)?

Procurement wants an activation playbook (PDF) and a concise one-page SLA impact summary we can attach to the RFP submission. Could you share a draft playbook we can review in the next week? Also, if you have a short preferred window (maintenance vs. immediate switchover) note that too.

Appreciate a point-by-point so we can inline answers into the questionnaire.

Regards,
Lydia Park
Head of Ops — Cloud Platform
Pioneer Financial

From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
To: Lydia Park <lydia.park@pioneerfinancial.com>
Cc: Avery Johnson <avery_johnson@redwood.ai>, Procurement Team <procurement@pioneerfinancial.com>
Date: Tue, 24 Nov 2026 09:07:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Activation playbook: staging cutover constraints

Lydia — thanks, this is very helpful. High level answers below; Avery and the reliability team will attach a playbook draft and sequence matrix for your review.

- RTO / RPO: we typically aim for an application-level RTO of 5–15 minutes for traffic cutover (control-plane and routing); full data-plane consistency (if customers use our managed replication) is generally restored within 1–10 minutes depending on commit durability settings. Worst-case (large stateful migrations, key rotation, or queued tokens) we plan for up to 1 hour for manual reconciliation.

- Replication mode: cross-region replication is asynchronous by default (log-based streaming). Median lag for steady-state workloads is ~10–40s; spikes to a few minutes under heavy sustained write load. For lower RPO we can enable a near-synchronous configuration (write-through replication) at the cost of higher write latency and increased egress.

- Cache / KV: KV caches are considered ephemeral — a failover will clear in-memory caches; we provide automated prefix warming and hint-based prefetching in the playbook. For session-critical workloads we recommend a short read-only window and a staged traffic ramp to allow caches to repopulate without errors.

- KMS: customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) are not automatically replicated between regions. We support key import/replication best practices in the playbook; for full PKI-handshake continuity we recommend pre-provisioning keys in target regions or using an HSM federation pattern to avoid automated downtime.

- Fallbacks: smart-routing policies enable automatic fallback to compatible model variants (lower memory/quantization) or to a reserved dedicated pool we can hold for incidents. We document escalation and traffic-throttling policies in the playbook.

I asked Avery to produce the activation-playbook-v1.pdf and a switchover matrix with the sequencing and estimated durations. Can your team review and flag any required compliance evidence we should attach?

I'll hold a 30-minute sync next week if that helps — propose Wed 12:00pm PT.

Thanks,
Sean Gallagher
Enterprise Sales — Redwood Inference

FYI — attaching the first draft of the activation playbook and the switchover sequencing spreadsheet. Key excerpts pasted below. Please review and we can iterate.

[Attachment: activation-playbook-v1.pdf (application/pdf)]
[Attachment: switchover-sequence.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)]

--- playbook excerpt ---
Overview:
- Purpose: stepwise activation for tenant-level regional failover (staging -> primary). Intended for customers using Redwood-hosted inference with optional dedicated pools.
- Expected window: 15–45 minutes for routine failover; up to 90 minutes for manual edge-case recovery.

Sequencing (high level):
1) Pre-cutover validation (0–5m): health checks, key material verification, capacity reservation, and cache snapshot marker.
2) Pause non-critical workloads (0–3m): throttle/pause bulk scoring jobs to reduce replication pressure.
3) Replicate final write-lag marker (1–2m): ensure write-ahead logs flushed to streaming pipeline.
4) Traffic switch (1–5m): update smart-router entries and DNS TTL handover; route verification probes.
5) Cache warm-up and shadow traffic (5–20m): warm caches with historical prefixes and replay small percentage of traffic to target region.
6) Post-cutover verification (5–15m): perf checks, token validation, and audit log capture.

RTO / RPO specifics:
- Typical RTO (control + traffic routing): 5 minutes.
- Conservative RTO: 15 minutes (accounts for DNS propagation and cache warm-up).
- Typical RPO for streaming replication: 10–60 seconds depending on workload; with near-sync mode achievable <5s.
- For persisted customer data that relies on third-party storage (S3, DB) RPO is dependent on the backing store replication settings — document outlines steps to verify.

KMS & Secrets:
- Pre-provision keys in target region or follow HSM-federation flow. If keys are not pre-provisioned, re-keying adds 20–40 minutes to the failover window.

Fallbacks and throttling:
- Automatic model-variant fallback to quantized variants if GPU capacity unavailable.
- Route to dedicated reserved capacity (if purchased) as a priority path.
- If neither is available, an automatic degraded-mode returns structured error responses with a service degradation header for customer-side handling.

--- end excerpt ---

Avery
Product Ops — Redwood Inference

Thanks — the deck is helpful. A couple quick clarifications before we share with Compliance:

- You mention cache warm-up / shadow traffic. Can Redwood guarantee no request-level errors (e.g., 5xx) during the warm-up window if we stage traffic at 10%?
- For RPO under steady state you list 10–60s. Procurement wants a clear best-effort number we can include. Is 30s conservative?
- SLA credits: Procurement asked what exceptions (if any) are written into the SLA for cross-region failovers initiated by the customer vs. automated platform failovers.

If you can answer these three bullets we can finalize the RFP appendix.

Lydia

From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Lydia Park <lydia.park@pioneerfinancial.com>, Avery Johnson <avery_johnson@redwood.ai>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 30 Nov 2026 15:02:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Fwd: Draft activation playbook and sequencing (v1)

Lydia — answering inline below (quoting your bullets):

> - You mention cache warm-up / shadow traffic. Can Redwood guarantee no request-level errors (e.g., 5xx) during the warm-up window if we stage traffic at 10%?

Short answer: we cannot guarantee zero 5xxs during warm-up because failures can stem from traffic patterns, model-variant OOMs, or third-party downstreams. What we *can* guarantee operationally:
- During staged ramp we run active probes and circuit breakers; if error rate crosses threshold (default 1.5% 5xx over 1 minute) we automatically rollback routing to source region.
- With the recommended staged ramp (10% -> 30% -> 60% over 15 minutes) we have observed <0.5% 5xx in our internal rehearsals for comparable workloads.

> - For RPO under steady state you list 10–60s. Procurement wants a clear best-effort number we can include. Is 30s conservative?

Yes — using our default streaming replication configuration, 30 seconds is a conservative best-effort RPO for most tenant workloads. If you enable the near-sync mode we can target <5s at the cost noted earlier. We'll document the exact trade-offs in the SLA appendix.

> - SLA credits: Procurement asked what exceptions (if any) are written into the SLA for cross-region failovers initiated by the customer vs. automated platform failovers.

Policy summary:
- For platform-initiated failovers (Redwood-detected outages and automatic policy-triggered switchover), SLA credits apply per the standard continuity SLA.
- For customer-initiated cutovers (manual activation for maintenance, DR testing), credits are not provided for the event window if the customer initiated the action and it is declared in advance or via an API call.
- Exceptions: if a customer initiates a cutover and we detect a platform-side misconfiguration that prolongs recovery beyond agreed thresholds, we will review case-by-case and may apply credits.

Next steps: we will update the playbook header to include the 30s best-effort RPO and the staged-ramp suggested percentages and will draft the one-page SLA impact summary for Procurement.

Regards,
Neha Kapoor
Reliability Engineering — Redwood Inference
